title: Windowing Large Lists
description: Master windowing and virtualization techniques to render large datasets efficiently with React Query.

data.text: Welcome to this comprehensive guide on **Windowing Large Lists**. Master windowing and virtualization techniques to render large datasets efficiently with React Query. In today's rapidly evolving technology landscape, understanding this topic is crucial for any developer looking to build robust, scalable, and maintainable applications. This lesson will take you from fundamental concepts to advanced implementations, providing you with practical knowledge you can apply immediately. Whether you are a beginner taking your first steps or an experienced developer looking to deepen your expertise, this guide has something valuable for you. We will explore theoretical foundations, practical implementations, real-world scenarios, and common pitfalls to avoid. By the end of this lesson, you will have a thorough understanding of Windowing Large Lists and be confident in applying it to your projects.
Why Windowing Matters

A list of 10,000 items means 10,000 DOM elements. Each element carries event listeners, styles, and memory overhead. Even with React's reconciliation, the initial paint and subsequent scroll events become janky. Windowing solves this by rendering only ~20-30 items at a time, regardless of total data size.

data.title: Do not window small lists
data.text: Windowing adds complexity. Only apply it when you expect more than 100-200 visible items. For smaller lists, standard mapping is faster and simpler.

data.text: Integrating react-window with React Query

Libraries like `react-window` and `react-virtuoso` handle the math of viewport calculation and DOM recycling. The key integration point is feeding the cached query data into the windowed list. React Query fetches and caches the full dataset; the windowing library handles rendering.

data.title: Fixed-size list with react-window
data.content: Rendering a large list of users using React Query data and react-window.

data.text: Variable-size Lists

Some lists have rows of varying height. `react-window` provides `VariableSizeList` for this scenario. You must measure or estimate row heights upfront. Alternatively, `react-virtuoso` auto-detects row sizes, making it a better choice for dynamic content like chat messages or cards with multiline text.

data.text: Infinite Scroll with Virtualization

When you combine infinite queries with windowing, you get an infinite scroll that stays performant. React Query's `useInfiniteQuery` fetches pages; the windowing library renders only what is visible. The integration requires calculating total item count from `data.pages` and flattening the nested page structure.

data.content: Combining useInfiniteQuery with a virtualized list for smooth infinite scroll.

items.text: Measure or estimate row heights before choosing a library
items.hint: Variable-size lists need accurate measurements for smooth scrolling.

items.text: Keep React Query fetching logic separate from windowing rendering logic
items.hint: Query fetches pages; windowing renders what is visible.

items.text: Flatten infinite query pages before passing to the list component
items.hint: useInfiniteQuery returns nested pages; windowing expects a flat array.

items.text: Trigger fetchNextPage when the user is within 5-10 items of the end
items.hint: Fetching too early wastes requests; too late causes visible loading.

items.text: Show a loading indicator at the bottom when fetching the next page
items.hint: Users need feedback that more content is coming.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Windowing renders only visible items, not the full dataset
Pair react-window or react-virtuoso with useQuery or useInfiniteQuery
Flatten infinite query pages before feeding them to the list
Choose react-virtuoso when row heights are dynamic
data.takeaway: Windowing keeps large lists performant by trading DOM nodes for scroll math.

data.text: Performance Considerations

Performance is a critical aspect of any production application. When implementing **Windowing Large Lists**, consider these optimization strategies to ensure your application remains fast and responsive:

items: **Lazy Loading**: Defer non-critical operations until they are actually needed to reduce initial load time.
**Caching**: Implement intelligent caching strategies to avoid redundant computations and network requests.
**Memoization**: Cache results of expensive function calls to improve performance for repeated operations.
**Batch Processing**: Group multiple operations together to reduce overhead and improve throughput.
**Resource Management**: Properly clean up resources, event listeners, and subscriptions to prevent memory leaks.
**Profiling**: Use performance profiling tools to identify bottlenecks before optimizing.
**Bundle Size**: Minimize dependencies and use tree-shaking to reduce application bundle size.
**Network Optimization**: Reduce payload sizes, use compression, and implement efficient data fetching strategies.

data.text: Security Considerations
Security should never be an afterthought. When implementing **Windowing Large Lists**, keep these security best practices in mind to protect your application and users:

items: **Input Validation**: Always validate and sanitize user input to prevent injection attacks.
**Authentication and Authorization**: Implement proper access controls and verify user permissions.
**Secrets Management**: Never hardcode API keys, passwords, or tokens. Use environment variables and secret management services.
**HTTPS**: Always use HTTPS in production to encrypt data in transit.
**Content Security Policy**: Implement CSP headers to mitigate XSS attacks.
**Dependency Scanning**: Regularly scan dependencies for known vulnerabilities.
**Rate Limiting**: Protect APIs from abuse with appropriate rate limiting.
**Audit Logging**: Log security-relevant events for monitoring and incident response.
